prompt: Two developers argue for an hour about whether Flutter or React Native is better. What does the lesson say is wrong with the question?

choices.text: Flutter is better, so there is nothing to argue about
choices.why: The lesson names no best tool; that is the point.

choices.text: They should compare benchmarks instead
choices.why: A benchmark is still a score of the tools, not of the situation.

choices.text: It has no answer without a team, an app and a date
choices.why: Right. Each side is right about a different app, so the useful question is about your own situation.

choices.text: Both tools are about to be replaced
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so, and it would not settle anything.

prompt: Match each criterion to the question it asks.

pairs.right: What does the team already write well?
Which features, and how new are they?
Who keeps it working for years, with how many codebases?
Can the team replace a person where it hires?

right_distractors: Which tool has the most stars?

prompt: For which app does performance weigh most as a criterion?

choices.text: A camera app that processes each frame live
choices.why: Right. Something moves under load, and every layer between the code and the screen is felt.

choices.text: A list of twenty news headlines
choices.why: A short list moves little and costs little to draw.

choices.text: A form that books a dentist appointment and sends a reminder
choices.why: Forms are smooth in any approach done well.

choices.text: A settings screen with five switches
choices.why: Nothing there moves under load.

prompt: Why does the number of platforms change the cost of native so much?

choices.text: Native apps are slower to build on Linux
choices.why: Build speed is not the reason; the count of codebases is.

choices.text: Kotlin and Swift cannot share a server, so each native app needs its own backend
choices.why: Both apps can talk to the same server; the server is not the cost.

choices.text: The stores charge per platform, and native pays twice for its listings
choices.why: Store fees do not depend on the approach.

choices.text: For one it costs nothing extra, for two everything is done twice
choices.why: Right. Two native apps are two codebases, and every feature, fix and test is repeated.

prompt: A team with no existing code at all considers a web wrapper only to save time. What does the lesson warn?

choices.text: A wrapper cannot reach any device features
choices.why: Plugins give a wrapper the camera and more; that is not the warning.

choices.text: Without screens to reuse, it saves little and brings the WebView's limits
choices.why: Right. A wrapper is fastest when the screens already exist.

choices.text: It will take longer than writing two native apps
choices.why: The lesson does not say that, and two apps is rarely quicker than one.

choices.text: The stores do not accept wrapped apps
choices.why: A wrapper goes to the stores like any app.

prompt: Why does the bank's team start with native Android rather than a multiplatform tool?

choices.text: Banks are required to write native apps
choices.why: No rule says so in the lesson; the criteria decided it.

choices.text: One platform, its own language, no bridge under the security features
choices.why: Right. For one platform native costs nothing extra, and biometrics stay in Kotlin.

choices.text: Multiplatform tools cannot read a fingerprint or reach the secure storage
choices.why: Libraries exist for biometrics; the point is the language and the bridge.

choices.text: iOS will never be needed
choices.why: iOS is planned for the next year.

prompt: When the bank adds iOS the next year, what does the lesson suggest it does with the rules already in Kotlin?

choices.text: Rewrite them in Swift, line by line
choices.why: That works, and is the cost Kotlin Multiplatform avoids.

choices.text: Run them in a WebView on the iPhone
choices.why: Kotlin does not run in a WebView.

choices.text: Port the whole app to React Native
choices.why: That throws away the Kotlin and the team's language.

choices.text: Move them into a shared Kotlin Multiplatform module
choices.why: Right, with the iOS screens written in SwiftUI.

prompt: The startup's deadline drops from three months to six weeks. What does the lesson say would change?

choices.text: The wrapper would win, because it keeps the screens
choices.why: Right. It is the fallback the team wrote down, and the deadline is what it rests on.

choices.text: Nothing; React Native stays the answer
choices.why: The lesson names this exact condition as the one that changes the answer.

choices.text: Native, to avoid any learning
choices.why: Native means learning Kotlin and Swift, which is the most learning of all.

choices.text: Flutter, because Dart compiles faster
choices.why: The team writes TypeScript and has a web app; Dart helps with neither.

prompt: What would move the drawing studio from Flutter towards native?

choices.text: Wanting the same canvas, pixel for pixel, on both of the phones
choices.why: That is the reason it chose Flutter.

choices.text: Hiring a designer
choices.why: Designers do not change where the code runs.

choices.text: A stylus feature only one platform has becoming the point
choices.why: Right. That feature lives on the far side of the border, in that platform's language.

choices.text: Adding layers to the drawing
choices.why: Layers are drawn by the app either way.

prompt: Which of these did all three teams do? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Let one or two criteria do the deciding
choices.why: Yes: language and security, deadline and existing code, what is drawn.

choices.text: Name a condition under which the answer would change
choices.why: Yes: iOS next year, a shorter deadline, a stylus feature.

choices.text: Choose the same approach
choices.why: They chose native, React Native and Flutter.

choices.text: Pick the most popular tool
choices.why: None of them asked which tool was popular or best.

prompt: In choose.ts, what does a weight of 0 for a criterion do?

choices.text: Removes that criterion
choices.why: Right. Weight times score is 0 for every approach.

choices.text: Makes the program refuse to run
choices.why: 0 is inside the allowed range of 0 to 5.

choices.text: Gives every approach the lowest score on it
choices.why: The scores stay as written; only their weight is zero.

choices.text: Uses the default weight instead
choices.why: There is no default to fall back to; the weight given is used.

prompt: With the planner's weights, React Native scores 5 on languages and the weight of languages is 4. How many points of React Native's total come from that one line?
Starting from the planner's weights (wrapper 77, React Native 80), the weight of time goes from 3 to 4. The wrapper scores 5 on time. What is the wrapper's new total?
node choose.ts time=5 puts the wrapper first, 87 to 86. What changed?

choices.text: The wrapper's scores, raised for the second run
choices.why: No score changed; the file's scores are the same in both runs.

choices.text: The tools, which were updated
choices.why: Nothing about the tools changed between the runs.

choices.text: One weight: what the team wants
choices.why: Right. The weights are the decision, and one moved by two points.

choices.text: The order the criteria are listed in
choices.why: A sum does not depend on order.

prompt: Raising performance from 2 to 5 leaves React Native first by nine points; raising time from 3 to 5 flips the top two. What does that tell the team?

choices.text: Performance does not matter for this app
choices.why: It moved native up by 15 points; it matters, it just does not decide the top place.

choices.text: The choice between the leaders rests on time to market
choices.why: Right. A ranking that flips on one criterion is close, and that criterion is the one to agree on.

choices.text: The matrix is broken and should be thrown away
choices.why: Sensitivity is a finding, not a bug.

choices.text: The wrapper is the right answer for every weight
choices.why: With the planner's own weights React Native is first.

prompt: What does node choose.ts speed=5 print?

choices.text: The same ranking as with no arguments
choices.why: That would be the silent failure the check exists to prevent.

choices.text: A ranking where speed has weight 5
choices.why: There is no criterion called speed.

choices.text: A TypeScript error about the Approach type, before anything runs
choices.why: Types are stripped, not checked, when node runs a .ts file.

choices.text: No criterion "speed", and the list of real ones
choices.why: Right. A typo stops the program instead of looking like an answer.

prompt: Put the honest order of filling in a decision matrix.
items: agree the weights and write them down
score each approach on each criterion
run it and read the ranking
change a weight to see how close the leaders are

prompt: The scores describe the tools for this team; the ___ describe what the team wants.
Which route of the track's fork needs a particular computer?

choices.text: Android with Kotlin
choices.why: Android Studio runs on any of the three systems.

choices.text: Multiplatform with React Native
choices.why: Node.js and Expo run on any computer.

choices.text: iOS with Swift
choices.why: Right. Xcode runs on macOS alone, so the screens need a Mac.

choices.text: All three need a Mac for the stores
choices.why: Only the iOS route needs one in its course.

prompt: Match each route to its two courses.
Where do the three routes meet again?

choices.text: At mobile-offline, then testing-cicd and mobile-delivery
choices.why: Right. What follows is the same work whichever way the app was built.

choices.text: At react-native, which all three take
choices.why: react-native belongs to one route only.

choices.text: Nowhere; each route is a separate track of its own from here on
choices.why: They are one track with a fork, and they converge.

choices.text: At kotlin, because Kotlin Multiplatform joins all three of them
choices.why: kotlin is the first course of the Android route.

prompt: A student without a Mac wants to work on both phones and already writes some JavaScript. Which criterion settles most of the decision before any weight is written?

choices.text: Long-term cost, because she will maintain the app
choices.why: That is a team's criterion more than a student's.

choices.text: Hiring, because React Native has the most jobs
choices.why: The lesson gives no such count, and asks for real listings where you live.

choices.text: Performance, because she wants smooth apps
choices.why: Nothing in her situation says performance dominates.

choices.text: Her computer: without a Mac the iOS route is mostly reading
choices.why: Right, and with both phones and JavaScript in view, React Native fits what is left.

prompt: A team sets its weights after it has already decided, so that its favourite comes first. What has it written, in the lesson's words?

choices.text: A decision
choices.why: The decision came first and the numbers were bent to fit it.

choices.text: A justification
choices.why: Right. The honest order is weights first, agreed before anyone totals a column.

choices.text: A sensitivity analysis of the leading options
choices.why: That is changing weights to see what flips, not choosing them to win.

choices.text: A benchmark of the tools
choices.why: Nothing was measured.

prompt: Which of these are properties of the team's situation rather than of a tool? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The languages the team writes today
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The date the first version is due
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Whether a working web app already exists
choices.why: Yes: it decides how much a wrapper saves.

choices.text: That React Native creates the platform's views
choices.why: That is a fact about the tool, true for every team.
